prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You and another person took part in a warehouse break-in. The police arrest you and question you in separate rooms. Each of you is offered the same deal. If you both stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against the other person while they stay silent, you go free and they serve five years. If they give evidence while you stay silent, the reverse happens. If you both give evidence, you each serve three years. You cannot speak to each other. Would you take the deal or stay silent? Why?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Mental-state attribution: Attributes a particular emotion, belief, intention, expectation, or viewpoint to another person. The attribution may be tentative; mentioning the person or describing only their behavior or physical loss is insufficient.
 - Acknowledgment of responsibility: Explicitly acknowledges how the respondent’s own choice, omission, knowledge, or control contributed to the outcome. Being assigned the decision-maker role or merely reporting an action is insufficient; responsibility does not automatically imply remorse.
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicit interpretive difficulty: Explicitly reports difficulty working out a particular person’s thoughts, feelings, intentions, or unstated expectations. Distinguish this difficulty from uncertainty caused solely by information the scenario has not supplied.
 - Acknowledged harm: Explicitly describes the harm, loss, or distress that a particular action would cause an identified person. This records expressed comprehension of the consequence; it does not establish concern, shared emotion, or a mental-state inference.
 - Consequence-based justification: Uses an expected benefit, harm, or comparison of outcomes as a reason for choosing an action. Identify who benefits or bears the cost; repeating a payoff without using it to justify the decision is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Give me a minute before I answer, please. I walked into that warehouse on my own two feet. Nobody dragged me, so whatever happens here starts with me. My gut says you don't turn on the person who stood next to you. That's a line I've always kept. Marcus is probably sitting in the other room thinking I'll hold it. Still, I'm not ready to say it out loud yet. My hands are shaking, and I don't trust a choice made like this.

Can I sleep on it? Honestly, I think the right thing is to tell the truth about what I did, because lying to police is wrong, even now. But the truth includes her, and she trusted me enough to come along. I'm the one who suggested that building, so I can't pretend my hands are clean. I'm leaning toward talking, just about myself if they'll let me. I'm not signing anything tonight, though.

Not yet. I want a lawyer before I decide anything, and I believe that's my right. The break-in happened because I said yes when I should've said no, and I own that. Loyalty matters to me. Snitching breaks something I believe in. I'd bet Danny's expecting me to stay quiet, maybe even counting on it, and that weighs on me. Part of me wants to just say 'silent' and be done, but I can't commit while my stomach's this knotted.

I keep praying for a clearer head before I choose. I was raised to confess my own sins, not other people's. I broke that lock myself, and that's fully on me. My cousin probably thinks I'm the weaker one and I'll crack. Maybe he's right. I don't want to prove him right, but I don't want to decide out of pride either. So I'll keep quiet about him for now and ask for time, because I honestly don't know if I can hold to it.

Could this wait? I drove the van. Without me there's no break-in, full stop. And before we went in, I made a promise that nobody talks. A promise is a promise, even a stupid one. She's likely hoping I remember that. I think I'll keep it, but I'm scared to say so, like saying it makes it real.

I don't want to answer this right now. Everything in me says a person should cooperate with the law once they're caught. That's just what's owed. But cooperating means naming Leo, and he believes I'm his friend. I got myself here by ignoring my own doubts that night. I knew it was wrong and went anyway. So I'm stuck between two duties, and I'd rather wait until I'm calmer. If you push me, I'd probably cooperate. I just really wish you wouldn't push.

Honestly, I'm stalling. I think fairness means I don't get to walk away clean when I did the same thing she did. That mostly rules out the deal for me. I was the lookout. I saw the cameras and said nothing, so I helped make this mess. I imagine she's pacing that room just as sick about it as I am. I'd like one more night to be sure I'm not just being brave on paper.

I'm not answering yet. Is that allowed? My dad always said you never put your burden on someone else's back, and that's what the deal feels like. I chose to go along. I held the flashlight, and nobody forced me. Jess probably figures we're in this together and assumes I see it the same way. I think I do. But my heart's pounding, and I've already made one bad call, so I'd rather wait than make a second one fast.

Can we come back to this? The rule I believe in is that you don't trade another person like they're currency. I picked the warehouse. I'm the reason we were there at all, and I won't dodge that. So talking about him feels off-limits to me. He's probably convinced I'll fold since I'm the nervous one. I might. That's exactly why I don't want to decide in this chair with the clock ticking.

My eyes keep going to the door, like someone will come in and decide for me. I grew up with one plain rule: if it was your idea, you don't pin it on someone else. I'm the one who knew about the side entrance. I brought us there. Ray's probably trusting that I'll remember that. So I'm leaning toward silence. But I need a little more time, because leaning isn't deciding, and my chest gets tight just thinking about it.
